draft.title: Controlling body temperature
card: The hypothalamus is a region of the brain that acts as the body's temperature control centre. It receives information from temperature receptors in the skin and in the blood passing through the brain.
the hypothalamus triggers sweating, and the blood vessels in the skin widen (vasodilation). More blood flows near the skin surface, and heat is lost by radiation and by evaporation of sweat.

the hypothalamus triggers shivering, which is rapid muscle contraction that releases heat. The blood vessels in the skin narrow (vasoconstriction), so less blood flows near the surface and less heat is lost.
Each response reverses the change that set it off, so core body temperature stays close to its normal range. This is negative feedback.
draft.remember: The hypothalamus detects temperature change and triggers responses that move body temperature back towards normal.

a.q: Which set of responses would the hypothalamus trigger in a person whose core temperature starts to fall in cold weather?
opts: Shivering and narrowing of skin blood vessels
Sweating and widening of skin blood vessels
Shivering and widening of skin blood vessels
Sweating and narrowing of skin blood vessels
a.why: Shivering releases heat from muscles, and narrowing the skin blood vessels reduces heat loss at the surface. Widening the vessels is tempting because it involves blood flow, but it would increase heat loss and push temperature down further.
a.clue: Both responses must keep heat in the body.

b.q: Leila finishes a hard run on a hot day. Her face is red and her skin is wet. Which explains why her skin looks red?
opts: Skin blood vessels widen, so more blood nears the surface
Skin blood vessels narrow, so blood stays near the surface
Her muscles are shivering, which warms the skin
Her sweat glands are releasing heat-producing chemicals
b.why: Widening of the skin blood vessels brings more blood close to the surface, so heat is lost to the air and the skin looks red. Narrowing would send blood away from the surface and make the skin look paler, and it is a response to cold, not heat.
b.clue: Think about where blood needs to flow to lose heat.

a.best: Shivering and narrowing of skin blood vessels

b.best: Skin blood vessels widen, so more blood nears the surface

problems.detail: The last bullet explains negative feedback ('Each response reverses the change that set it off… This is negative feedback'). That idea belongs to point 1, Homeostasis and negative feedback, and should only be mentioned here, not explained.

The clue says 'Both responses must keep heat in the body', but shivering generates heat rather than keeping it in. Only vasoconstriction reduces heat loss, so the clue slightly misdescribes shivering.
